Leannoth
lee-AN-noth
n. (Hebrew; part of the musical direction in the title of the eighty-eighth psalm)
Hebrew le-'annoth, for afflicting or to humble, from anah, to afflict or bow down; left untranslated by the Authorized Version in the title of Psalm 88, where it follows Mahalath.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Leannoth is the second half of the musical direction the Authorized Version leaves standing over the eighty-eighth psalm: “A Song or Psalm for the sons of Korah, to the chief Musician upon Mahalath Leannoth, Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite. O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee” (Psalm 88:1). Mahalath is sickness, and Leannoth comes from the Hebrew verb to afflict or to bow down, so the pair reads roughly concerning sickness, for afflicting — a tune or a manner of singing fitted to grief. The title is honest advertising. This is the darkest psalm in the Psalter. The singer asks only to be heard: “Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry” (Psalm 88:2); he reports his condition plainly: “For my soul is full of troubles: and my life draweth nigh unto the grave” (Psalm 88:3); and he ends without relief: “Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness” (Psalm 88:18). That the congregation of Israel was given a song for affliction which does not resolve is a mercy. God made room in His own hymnbook for the believer who sees no morning yet.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Leannoth is a Hebrew term left untranslated in Scripture and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Leannoth is a Hebrew word; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

It appears once, in the title of Psalm 88.

It follows Mahalath, which signifies sickness.

It comes from anah, to afflict or to bow down.

The psalm it heads is the darkest in the Psalter.

Key Scripture

Psa 88:1 — "A Song or Psalm for the sons of Korah, to the chief Musician upon Mahalath Leannoth, Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite. O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee:"

Psa 88:2 — "Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;"

Psa 88:3 — "For my soul is full of troubles: and my life draweth nigh unto the grave."

Psa 88:18 — "Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness."

Modern Corruption

Grief is treated as a failure of faith; Leannoth labels an inspired song of affliction that never resolves.

expand to see more

Much modern worship has no room for a believer in the dark. A song must end in a lifted chorus, and a saint who cannot sing it is quietly judged. The eighty-eighth psalm was given to the chief musician with a direction for affliction, and it ends with acquaintance put into darkness. God does not require His people to lie about their condition before He will hear them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that lament is an appointed form of worship, that a psalm may end unresolved and still be inspired, and that crying day and night before God is faith and not its failure.
